hero.heading: What this hub is, and who it is for
hero.body: The Firehouse is NOAA's Global Systems Laboratory's public hub for fire weather social science. It gathers what completed research has already established about end-user needs and recommendations, so the next project, product or conversation can start from known unmet needs instead of rediscovering the same gaps.

mission.heading: Why it exists
paragraphs: Fire weather social science asks what partners and the public actually need from weather information when decisions can't wait. A lot of great research exists, but its findings usually stay trapped inside individual reports.

The Firehouse pulls those completed projects into a single collection—preserving the researchers' exact words, end-user needs, and recommendations. Then, analyzed collectively, these needs are distilled into the five most pressing issues across four core areas—observations, forecasts, warnings, and governance—and ranked by frequency. Every count comes directly from published work, every synthesis is human-reviewed, and every need names the projects that backed it.

audiences.heading: Built for the people who use fire weather information
audiences.body: The same body of evidence answers a different question depending on who is reading it.

items.title: Fire weather forecasters
items.body: See what the people receiving a forecast have said they need from it — timing, framing, lead time, delivery — and what has already been recommended about how it reaches them.

items.title: Researchers
items.body: Make your grant proposals bulletproof. Ground your next proposal in real, documented user needs rather than guesses or unintentional retreads. Easily see which topics are thoroughly supported and where the evidence is still thin, so you can clearly justify fresh research or a deliberate replication study.

items.title: Decision makers and land managers
items.body: Back up your pitch with real data. When you're pushing for a new tool, a product tweak, or a better way of working, point straight to the evidence—complete with the exact study, the year, and the researchers behind it.

process.heading: From a completed project to a published need

steps.title: Researchers submit completed work
steps.body: A short survey collects what was studied, where, at which point in the fire cycle, the major takeaways, the end-user needs and recommendations, and links to anything published. Submissions are open at any time. Each new submission will be reviewed before it is published to the website.

steps.title: The findings are synthesized and reviewed
steps.body: The needs recorded across every project are read together, grouped into the four topic areas and ranked by mentions. Each updated pass of the synthesis is reviewed as new projects roll in, before it is published.

steps.title: Everything stays traceable
steps.body: Each published need names the projects it draws on, and each project keeps a page of its own with the researchers' verbatim takeaways, needs and papers.

team.heading: Who is behind it
team.body: This whole thing is the brainchild of Stephanie and Emily. They run the surveys, personally review every synthesis pass before it gets published, and keep the records up to date.

members.name: Dr. Stephanie Hoekstra
bio: By day, Dr. Stephanie Hoekstra studies the human side of extreme weather—translating how people interpret risk and make high-stakes decisions when nature gets wild. Her current focus is all about fire weather, partnering directly with National Weather Service forecasters and wildland fire professionals to make sure decision-support tools are actually, genuinely useful in the heat of the moment. By night (and weekend), she trades risk communication for refereeing her three kids, playing ice hockey, endlessly scrolling Zillow floorplans she has no intention of buying, and pursuing a lifelong mission of finding the absolute best cannoli on Earth.

members.name: Dr. Emily Wells
bio: Dr. Emily Wells is a social and decision scientist with a deep curiosity about how wildland fire operational professionals make decisions under uncertainty, particularly when it comes to if and how they use advanced technologies. What motivates her most is engaging with practitioners: listening to their stories, learning from their perspectives, and translating their operational realities and needs back to researchers and model developers. Emily is a proud, born and raised Yinzer (here we go Steelers!). When her laptop is closed, you can find her swimming laps, hiking in the Rockies, or tuning into her guilty pleasure - reality TV.

cta.heading: Add your work to the record
cta.body: If you've wrapped up fire weather social science research, send it over. Your work will join the master record and inform our cross-project syntheses.
